newsitem.title: ANGOLA: SOUTHERN AFRICAN LEADERS CONDEMN ANGOLA'S SAVIMBI.
newsitem.headline: SOUTHERN AFRICAN LEADERS CONDEMN ANGOLA'S SAVIMBI.

text.p: Southern African leaders meeting in Luanda to help Angola's peace process condemned UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi on Wednesday for his failure to arrive, which dashed hopes of a quick breakthrough in the stalled initiative.

The 11 Southern African Development Community (SADC) leaders attending the one-day summit appealed to Savimbi's movement to fulfill its commitments in the Lusaka Protocol, signed by the Angolan government and UNITA in 1994 to end two decades of war.

In a joint statement, SADC also urged the United Nations' Security Council, which reviews its peace-keeping mandate in Angola on Thursday, to "develop measures which oblige UNITA to fully respect deadlines" in a peace timetable.
The meeting decided too that the region would send five ministers to the Security Council in New York to present SADC's position on the Angolan peace process.

Zimbabwe's President Robert Mugabe, chairman of SADC's political, defence and security council, said Savimbi had sent him a letter on Wednesday indicating his reasons for not attending the summit in the government-controlled capital.

"It is not for security reasons that he is not here. It is because of political conditions, which he wanted fulfilled and have not been met. This is the very reason we wanted him here, so he could tell us what those political conditions are.

"Those conditions can only be created through negotiations with the government. He and President (Jose Eduardo) dos Santos need to get together," Mugabe told a news conference shortly before the SADC leaders left Angola.
"Dr Savimbi is to blame for not being here. He has concluded he should be absent, and we condemn that and we hope he will not do it again in the future."
Mugabe said SADC wanted early talks between Savimbi and dos Santos and urged UNITA to commit itself to peace and democracy.

"We are now looking at the United Nations to use its own authority in helping the thrust of peace. It is now the international community which really must be supported here to help move forward the process," Mugabe said.
"We need greater pressure than perhaps the pressure that is there at the moment."
Southern African leaders are keen to see the Angolan peace process completed to ensure stability in the region, but it is has slowed almost to a stop.
While UNITA generals were integrated last month into the national army with their former enemies, political rapprochement has hardly begun.
Savimbi has rejected the vice-presidency reserved for him under the peace accord. It would have meant moving to government -held Luanda, far away from his northern Bailundo base.

The 12-member SADC comprises Mauritius, Angola, Lesotho, Swaziland, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Namibia, Mozambique, Tanzania, Malawi, Botswana and South Africa. Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa, currently visiting the U.S., did not attend the summit.
